claim: The transmembrane chemokines CX3CL1/fractalkine and CXCL16 are widely expressed in different types of tumors, often without an appropriate expression of their classical receptors.
source: The transmembrane chemokines CX3CL1/fractalkine and CXCL16 are widely expressed in different types of tumors, often without an appropriate expression of their classical receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, which demonstrates high expression of CXCL16 and CX3CL1 in various tumor cell lines while their receptors CXCR6 and CX3CR1 are absent or minimally expressed.

claim: Receptor-negative cancer cells expressing transmembrane chemokines can be stimulated by soluble chemokines.
source: We observed that receptor-negative cancer cells could be stimulated by the soluble chemokines.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3 showing ERK phosphorylation and biological effects in receptor-negative but tm-chemokine-positive cells upon stimulation with soluble chemokines.

claim: All cells expressing or transfected with transmembrane chemokine ligands bound the soluble chemokines with high affinity.
source: Searching for alternative receptors we detected that all cells expressing or transfected with transmembrane chemokine ligands bound the soluble chemokines with high affinity and responded by phosphorylation of intracellular kinases, enhanced proliferation and anti-apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by binding experiments shown in Figure 5, including fluorescence microscopy, FACS analysis, and electron microscopy demonstrating binding of soluble chemokines to tm-chemokine expressing cells.

claim: Cells expressing transmembrane chemokines respond to soluble chemokines by phosphorylation of intracellular kinases.
source: Searching for alternative receptors we detected that all cells expressing or transfected with transmembrane chemokine ligands bound the soluble chemokines with high affinity and responded by phosphorylation of intracellular kinases, enhanced proliferation and anti-apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figures 2, 6, and 8 showing ERK phosphorylation in tm-chemokine expressing cells upon stimulation with soluble chemokines.

claim: Soluble chemokines enhance proliferation of cells expressing transmembrane chemokines.
source: Searching for alternative receptors we detected that all cells expressing or transfected with transmembrane chemokine ligands bound the soluble chemokines with high affinity and responded by phosphorylation of intracellular kinases, enhanced proliferation and anti-apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by WST-assay data in Figure 3 showing increased proliferation of U343 and A764 glioma cells upon stimulation with soluble chemokines.

claim: Soluble chemokines induce anti-apoptotic effects in cells expressing transmembrane chemokines.
source: Searching for alternative receptors we detected that all cells expressing or transfected with transmembrane chemokine ligands bound the soluble chemokines with high affinity and responded by phosphorylation of intracellular kinases, enhanced proliferation and anti-apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by caspase-3/7 activity assays in Figure 3 and cleaved PARP measurements in Figure 7, showing reduced apoptosis in tm-chemokine expressing cells stimulated with soluble chemokines.

claim: The intracellular domain of transmembrane chemokines is required for inverse signaling activity.
source: This activity requires the intracellular domain and apparently the dimerization of the transmembrane chemokine ligand.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments in Figure 6B showing that C-terminally truncated tm-chemokines lacking the intracellular domain cannot transduce signals upon stimulation with soluble chemokines.

claim: Dimerization of transmembrane chemokines is required for inverse signaling.
source: This activity requires the intracellular domain and apparently the dimerization of the transmembrane chemokine ligand.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments in Figure 9 showing that intact antibodies but not monovalent F(ab) fragments can induce signaling, suggesting dimerization is necessary.

claim: CXCL16 and CX3CL1 are transmembrane proteins that are converted to soluble ligands by metalloproteinases, in particular ADAM10 and ADAM17.
source: The chemokines CX3CL1/fractalkine and CXCL16 are transmembrane (tm) proteins (Bazan et al., 1997; Matloubian et al., 2000) that are converted to soluble ligands by metalloproteinases, in particular ADAM10 and ADAM17 (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase, Garton et al., 2001; Hundhausen et al., 2003; Abel et al., 2004; Ludwig et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bazan et al., 1997; Matloubian et al., 2000; Garton et al., 2001; Hundhausen et al., 2003; Abel et al., 2004; Ludwig et al., 2005).

claim: Soluble chemokines induce signal transduction and chemotaxis in target cells which express their classical G protein-coupled receptors CX3CR1 and CXCR6/Bonzo.
source: These soluble (s-) chemokines induce signal transduction and chemotaxis in target cells which express their classical G protein-coupled receptors CX3CR1 and CXCR6/Bonzo; however, also firm adhesion between tm-chemokine- and chemokine-receptor-bearing cells has been reported (Imai et al., 1997; Wilbanks et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Imai et al., 1997; Wilbanks et al., 2001) describing classical chemokine receptor signaling.

claim: Both CX3CL1 and CXCL16 show potential signal transduction sites in their short intracellular domains.
source: Of note, both chemokines themselves, show potential signal transduction sites in their short intracellular domains, but so far signaling via the transmembrane forms has not been described (Bazan et al., 1997; Matloubian et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bazan et al., 1997; Matloubian et al., 2000) and is consistent with the sequence analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Signaling via the transmembrane forms of CX3CL1 and CXCL16 has not been previously described.
source: Of note, both chemokines themselves, show potential signal transduction sites in their short intracellular domains, but so far signaling via the transmembrane forms has not been described (Bazan et al., 1997; Matloubian et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of such descriptions in the cited literature (Bazan et al., 1997; Matloubian et al., 2000) and establishes the novelty of the current findings.

claim: Reverse signaling by transmembrane ligands has been initially observed with ligands of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) family after binding to their cognate receptors.
source: This reverse transduction of signals by transmembrane ligands has been initially observed with ligands of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) family after binding to their cognate receptors (or to antibodies), and thus bidirectional responses are produced (Ferran et al., 1994; Eissner et al., 2004; Lettau et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Ferran et al., 1994; Eissner et al., 2004; Lettau et al., 2011) describing reverse signaling in TNF family ligands.

claim: Reverse signaling has been described for IL-15.
source: This principle has been also described for IL-15 (Neely et al., 2004), ephrin-ligands (Klein, 2009) and semaphorins (Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Neely et al., 2004).

claim: Reverse signaling has been described for ephrin-ligands.
source: This principle has been also described for IL-15 (Neely et al., 2004), ephrin-ligands (Klein, 2009) and semaphorins (Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Klein, 2009).

claim: Reverse signaling has been described for semaphorins.
source: This principle has been also described for IL-15 (Neely et al., 2004), ephrin-ligands (Klein, 2009) and semaphorins (Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Zhou et al., 2008).

claim: Reverse signaling can induce co-stimulation, silencing, and transmission of additional signals.
source: Reverse signaling can induce several biological functions, e. g. co-stimulation, silencing, transmission of additional signals (Eissner et al., 2004; Sun and Fink, 2007), or synapse formation and plasticity in the nervous system (Klein, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Eissner et al., 2004; Sun and Fink, 2007).

claim: Reverse signaling can induce synapse formation and plasticity in the nervous system.
source: Reverse signaling can induce several biological functions, e. g. co-stimulation, silencing, transmission of additional signals (Eissner et al., 2004; Sun and Fink, 2007), or synapse formation and plasticity in the nervous system (Klein, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Klein, 2009).

claim: High levels of CXCL16 mRNA are detected in human glioma cell lines U118, U343, A172, A764, and T98G.
source: By quantitative RT-PCR we detected high levels of CXCL16 and CX3CL1 in human glioma, neuroblastoma, colon carcinoma, lower levels in breast cancer cells, and LOX melanoma cells produced very low or non-detectable mRNA amounts (Figure 1 upper panel; Δ CT in logarithmic scale, thus a 3.3 higher Δ CTvalue indicates a 10-fold lower expression).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 upper panel.

claim: High levels of CX3CL1 mRNA are detected in human glioma cell lines U118, U343, A172, A764, and T98G.
source: By quantitative RT-PCR we detected high levels of CXCL16 and CX3CL1 in human glioma, neuroblastoma, colon carcinoma, lower levels in breast cancer cells, and LOX melanoma cells produced very low or non-detectable mRNA amounts (Figure 1 upper panel; Δ CT in logarithmic scale, thus a 3.3 higher Δ CTvalue indicates a 10-fold lower expression).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 upper panel.

claim: High levels of CXCL16 and CX3CL1 mRNA are detected in neuroblastoma cells.
source: By quantitative RT-PCR we detected high levels of CXCL16 and CX3CL1 in human glioma, neuroblastoma, colon carcinoma, lower levels in breast cancer cells, and LOX melanoma cells produced very low or non-detectable mRNA amounts (Figure 1 upper panel; Δ CT in logarithmic scale, thus a 3.3 higher Δ CTvalue indicates a 10-fold lower expression).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 upper panel.

claim: High levels of CXCL16 and CX3CL1 mRNA are detected in colon carcinoma cells.
source: By quantitative RT-PCR we detected high levels of CXCL16 and CX3CL1 in human glioma, neuroblastoma, colon carcinoma, lower levels in breast cancer cells, and LOX melanoma cells produced very low or non-detectable mRNA amounts (Figure 1 upper panel; Δ CT in logarithmic scale, thus a 3.3 higher Δ CTvalue indicates a 10-fold lower expression).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 upper panel.

claim: Lower levels of CXCL16 and CX3CL1 mRNA are detected in breast cancer cells.
source: By quantitative RT-PCR we detected high levels of CXCL16 and CX3CL1 in human glioma, neuroblastoma, colon carcinoma, lower levels in breast cancer cells, and LOX melanoma cells produced very low or non-detectable mRNA amounts (Figure 1 upper panel; Δ CT in logarithmic scale, thus a 3.3 higher Δ CTvalue indicates a 10-fold lower expression).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 upper panel.

claim: LOX melanoma cells produce very low or non-detectable amounts of CXCL16 and CX3CL1 mRNA.
source: By quantitative RT-PCR we detected high levels of CXCL16 and CX3CL1 in human glioma, neuroblastoma, colon carcinoma, lower levels in breast cancer cells, and LOX melanoma cells produced very low or non-detectable mRNA amounts (Figure 1 upper panel; Δ CT in logarithmic scale, thus a 3.3 higher Δ CTvalue indicates a 10-fold lower expression).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 upper panel.

claim: Endothelial cells express CXCL16 and CX3CL1.
source: Beside tumor cells, also endothelial cells and monocytes like THP-1 cells express tm-chemokines.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 upper panel for HUVEC cells.

claim: Monocytic THP-1 cells express CXCL16 and CX3CL1.
source: Beside tumor cells, also endothelial cells and monocytes like THP-1 cells express tm-chemokines.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 upper panel for THP-1 cells.

claim: The expression of CXCR6 and CX3CR1 is restricted to only a few cell types, including activated T-cells and monocytes/monocytic THP-1 cells.
source: In contrast to this broad distribution of ligands, the expression of the receptors CXCR6 and CX3CR1 was restricted to only a few cell types, e.g. activated T-cells (positive control, compare Ludwig et al., 2005) or monocytes/monocytic THP-1 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 upper panel and citation to Ludwig et al., 2005.

claim: CXCR6 and CX3CR1 were not detectable in solid tumor cell lines on protein level by immunocytochemistry.
source: CXCR6 and CX3CR1 were not detectable in the solid tumor cell lines on protein level either (not shown) by immunocytochemistry using antibodies that were suitable for this application in recent investigations (Held-Feindt et al., 2010; Hattermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry experiments using antibodies validated in previous studies (Held-Feindt et al., 2010; Hattermann et al., 2013).

claim: Stimulation with s-CXCL16 or s-CX3CL1 induces transient, dose- and time-dependent phosphorylation of ERK kinases in receptor-negative, tm-chemokine-expressing cells.
source: When cells negative for the known receptors CXCR6 and CX3CL1 (compare Figure 1) were stimulated with s-CXCL16 or s-CX3CL1, we could, however, detect a transient, dose-and time-dependent phosphorylation of kinases and further biological effects (Figures 2A,B and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 2A and 2B demonstrating ERK phosphorylation.

claim: ERK phosphorylation in tm-chemokine-positive cells occurs after 10-40 min of stimulation with soluble chemokines.
source: In all tested cells that expressed tm-chemokines (like U343, A172, A764, T98G glioma cell lines, primary glioma cells, or HT29 colon carcinoma cells; not all shown) phosphorylation of ERKs (extracellular signal-regulated kinase, p42/p44) occurred after 10-40 min using concentrations from 0.01 to 10 nM with maximum responses at about 1 nM.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating time-dependent ERK phosphorylation.

claim: Maximum ERK phosphorylation responses occur at about 1 nM concentration of soluble chemokines.
source: In all tested cells that expressed tm-chemokines (like U343, A172, A764, T98G glioma cell lines, primary glioma cells, or HT29 colon carcinoma cells; not all shown) phosphorylation of ERKs (extracellular signal-regulated kinase, p42/p44) occurred after 10-40 min using concentrations from 0.01 to 10 nM with maximum responses at about 1 nM.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating dose-dependent ERK phosphorylation.

claim: LOX melanoma cells, which are tm-chemokine-negative and receptor-negative, show no signal transduction in response to soluble chemokines.
source: By contrast, in tm-chemokine-negative and receptor-negative LOX melanoma cells no signal transduction was observed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating absence of ERK phosphorylation in LOX cells.

claim: Primary glioma cells isolated from surgically dissected human gliomas are responsive to soluble chemokines.
source: Furthermore, not only cell lines but also primary cells isolated from surgically dissected human gliomas were responsive, which express – as the cell lines – tm-chemokines, but not their classical receptors (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating ERK phosphorylation in primary glioma cultures.

claim: Soluble chemokines (1 nM) enhance proliferation of U343 and A764 glioma cells expressing transmembrane counterparts.
source: Both chemokines, s-CXCL16 and s-CX3CL1, significantly enhanced proliferation of classical receptor-negative, tm-chemokine-positive cells like U343 or A764 glioma cells, whereas double-negative cells like LOX melanoma cells did not respond.
evidence: This claim is supported by WST-assay data shown in Figure 3 top panel.

claim: LOX melanoma cells, which are tm-chemokine-negative, do not show enhanced proliferation in response to soluble chemokines.
source: Both chemokines, s-CXCL16 and s-CX3CL1, significantly enhanced proliferation of classical receptor-negative, tm-chemokine-positive cells like U343 or A764 glioma cells, whereas double-negative cells like LOX melanoma cells did not respond.
evidence: This claim is supported by WST-assay data shown in Figure 3 top panel.

claim: Stimulation with s-CXCL16 and s-CX3CL1 reduces caspase-3/7 activity induced by Temozolomide in glioma cells.
source: Furthermore, stimulation with s-CXCL16 and s-CX3CL1 reduced caspase-3/7 activity that was induced by exposure to Temozolomide, a clinically used chemotherapeutic for gliomas.
evidence: This claim is supported by caspase-3/7 activity assay data shown in Figure 3 top panel.

claim: Soluble chemokines do not mediate cell migration in glioma cells.
source: However, the classical biological effect of chemokines, namely cell migration, was not mediated by this signaling (Figure 3 bottom, and Figure 3—source data 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by wound healing assay data shown in Figure 3 bottom panel.

claim: Pre-incubation with Pertussis toxin does not influence signal transduction of responsive tm-chemokine-positive cells stimulated with soluble chemokines.
source: Pre-incubation with Pertussis toxin did not influence signal transduction of responsive tm-chemokine-positive cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating ERK phosphorylation is maintained in the presence of Pertussis toxin.

claim: Pertussis toxin inhibits CX3CL1-mediated phosphorylation of Akt in CX3CR1-expressing THP-1 cells.
source: Its inhibitory effect was confirmed in stimulations of CX3CR1+-THP-1 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating that Pertussis toxin blocks Akt phosphorylation in THP-1 cells.

claim: An engineered peptide receptor-antagonist of fractalkine (F1) mediates ERK phosphorylation in primary glioma cells comparable to the recombinant soluble peptide.
source: Also, an engineered peptide receptor-antagonist of fractalkine (Hermand et al., 2008) mediated ERK phosphorylation in primary glioma cells comparable to the recombinant soluble peptide (Figure 4A, lower part).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A lower part and citation to Hermand et al., 2008.

claim: Glioma cell lines do not express CXCR3, CXCR4, CXCR6, or CX3CR1.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, glioma cell lines did not express CXCR3, CXCR4, CXCR6, CX3CR1, but high levels of CXCR7, which is a receptor for CXCL11 and CXCL12 and can mediate G-protein independent signals via arrestin (Odemis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Glioma cell lines express high levels of CXCR7.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, glioma cell lines did not express CXCR3, CXCR4, CXCR6, CX3CR1, but high levels of CXCR7, which is a receptor for CXCL11 and CXCL12 and can mediate G-protein independent signals via arrestin (Odemis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B and citation to Odemis et al., 2012.

claim: CXCR7 is a receptor for CXCL11 and CXCL12 and can mediate G-protein independent signals via arrestin.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, glioma cell lines did not express CXCR3, CXCR4, CXCR6, CX3CR1, but high levels of CXCR7, which is a receptor for CXCL11 and CXCL12 and can mediate G-protein independent signals via arrestin (Odemis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Odemis et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition of CXCR7 by the synthetic antagonist CCX733 has no influence on tm-chemokine signaling.
source: However, inhibition of CXCR7 by the synthetic antagonist (Hattermann et al., 2010; Yamaguchi et al., 2014) CCX733 exhibited no influence on tm-chemokine signaling (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C and citations to Hattermann et al., 2010 and Yamaguchi et al., 2014.

claim: Chemokine decoy receptors (D6, DARC, CCX-CKR) are expressed in glioma cells as well as LOX cells.
source: As chemokine decoy receptors (D6, DARC, CCX-CKR) were expressed in glioma as well as LOX cells, they could be ruled out as mediators for tm-chemokine effects that were absent in the melanoma cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The viral encoded putative receptor for CX3CL1, US28, was not detected in glioma cells or LOX melanoma cells.
source: A viral encoded putative receptor for CX3CL1, US28 (Matlaf et al., 2013), was detected neither in glioma cells, nor in LOX melanoma cells, and thus, can be excluded for s-CXCL16 or s-CX3CL1 signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B and citation to Matlaf et al., 2013.

claim: CD44 is expressed at comparable protein levels in glioma cells and melanoma cells.
source: Additionally, the expression of CD44, a receptor for hyaluronic acid and further ligands, e.g. CCL5 (Roscic-Mrkic et al., 2005)was determined at comparable protein levels in glioma cells and melanoma cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B and citation to Roscic-Mrkic et al., 2005.

claim: Fluorescent- or biotin-labeled s-CXCL16 or s-CX3CL1 bind to cells that express their tm-chemokine counterparts.
source: Fluorescent- or biotin-labeled s-CXCL16 or s-CX3CL1 bound to cells that express their tm-chemokine counterparts (as shown by fluorescence microscopy Figure 5A and FACS analysis Figure 5B), but not to tm-chemokine negative LOX cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 5A and FACS analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: Fluorescent- or biotin-labeled s-CXCL16 or s-CX3CL1 do not bind to tm-chemokine negative LOX cells.
source: Fluorescent- or biotin-labeled s-CXCL16 or s-CX3CL1 bound to cells that express their tm-chemokine counterparts (as shown by fluorescence microscopy Figure 5A and FACS analysis Figure 5B), but not to tm-chemokine negative LOX cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 5A and FACS analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: When LOX cells are transfected with tm-CXCL16 or tm-CX3CL1, binding of s-CXCL16 or s-CX3CL1 is clearly observed.
source: However, when LOX cells were transfected with tm-CXCL16 or tm-CX3CL1, binding of s-CXCL16 or s-CX3CL1 was clearly observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 5A and FACS analysis in Figure 5B showing binding in transfected LOX cells.

claim: Immuno-electron microscopy shows a close association between soluble and transmembrane chemokines on the cell surface.
source: The direct association of s- to tm-chemokines was also visualized by immuno-electron microscopy (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immuno-electron microscopy images shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Chemical cross-linking with paraformaldehyde shifts tm-chemokine bands to higher molecular weights when incubated with soluble chemokines.
source: A direct association of s-chemokines to tm-chemokines could also be verified by chemical cross-linking (Figure 5D). Isolated membranes from tm-chemokine transfected LOX cells were incubated with their corresponding s-chemokine (omitted in controls) and cross-linked by exposure to paraformaldehyde (PFA); then proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and blots incubated with antibodies to soluble chemokines. Only after cross-linking in the presence of s-chemokines a shift of the bands of tm-chemokines to higher molecular masses was observed, corresponding roughly to the binding of 1-2 soluble peptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D demonstrating band shifts after cross-linking.

claim: The band shift after cross-linking corresponds roughly to the binding of 1-2 soluble peptides to transmembrane chemokines.
source: Only after cross-linking in the presence of s-chemokines a shift of the bands of tm-chemokines to higher molecular masses was observed, corresponding roughly to the binding of 1-2 soluble peptides.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the molecular weight shifts observed in Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: LOX cells stably transfected with tm-CXCL16 or tm-CX3CL1 show time-dependent phosphorylation of ERK 1/2 upon stimulation with soluble chemokines.
source: Upon stimulation with soluble chemokines, transiently (not shown) as well as stably transfected cells showed a time dependent phosphorylation of ERK 1/2 (Figure 6A), which was not the case in non-transfected cells (compare Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Stably transfected LOX cells expressing C-terminally truncated tm-chemokine variants lacking the intracellular domain cannot be activated by stimulation with s-chemokines.
source: As the short intracellular domain of tm-chemokines could be involved in this signal transduction, we performed corresponding experiments with C-terminally truncated tm-chemokines that lacked the complete intracellular but not the transmembrane domain (Figure 6B). In fact, this truncation abolished the signal transduction effects observed with the full-length tm-chemokines.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B demonstrating absence of ERK phosphorylation in cells expressing truncated tm-chemokines.

claim: Conditioned media from tm-chemokine-transfected cells contain considerable amounts of corresponding s-chemokines.
source: In fact, 24 hr- or 48 hr-conditioned media of tm-chemokine-transfected cells, but not of vector-transfected cells, contained considerable amounts of corresponding s-chemokines as detected by Western blot or ELISA (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and ELISA data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Conditioned media from tm-chemokine-transfected cells induce ERK 1/2 phosphorylation in tm-chemokine-expressing cells.
source: As expected, conditioned media from transfected, but not from control cells, induced ERK 1/2 phosphorylation; again non- or control-transfected LOX cells yielded no signal transduction (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Stimulation of tm-CXCL16-transfected LOX cells with s-CXCL16 significantly reduces the amount of cleaved PARP induced by Camptothecin.
source: As shown by immunocytochemistry and Western blot, stimulation of tm-CXCL16-transfected LOX cells with s-CXCL16 and tm-CX3CL1-transfected LOX cells with s-CX3CL1 significantly reduced the amount of the cleaved Poly (ADP-Ribose) Polymerase (PARP), whereas mock-transfected LOX cells were not rescued (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Stimulation of tm-CX3CL1-transfected LOX cells with s-CX3CL1 significantly reduces the amount of cleaved PARP induced by Camptothecin.
source: As shown by immunocytochemistry and Western blot, stimulation of tm-CXCL16-transfected LOX cells with s-CXCL16 and tm-CX3CL1-transfected LOX cells with s-CX3CL1 significantly reduced the amount of the cleaved Poly (ADP-Ribose) Polymerase (PARP), whereas mock-transfected LOX cells were not rescued (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mock-transfected LOX cells are not rescued from Camptothecin-induced cell death by soluble chemokines.
source: As shown by immunocytochemistry and Western blot, stimulation of tm-CXCL16-transfected LOX cells with s-CXCL16 and tm-CX3CL1-transfected LOX cells with s-CX3CL1 significantly reduced the amount of the cleaved Poly (ADP-Ribose) Polymerase (PARP), whereas mock-transfected LOX cells were not rescued (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: siRNA silencing reduces tm-chemokine transcript amounts to 24-59% of controls transfected with unspecific control siRNAs.
source: By siRNA silencing, tm-chemokine transcript amounts were reduced up to 24-59% of controls transfected with unspecific control siRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8.

claim: s-chemokine-mediated ERK-phosphorylation is clearly reduced in tm-chemokine silenced cells.
source: The s-chemokine-mediated ERK-phosphorylation could be observed in control siRNA-treated glioma cell lines and primary cultures but was clearly reduced in tm-chemokine silenced cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Specific antibodies against the chemokine domains of CXCL16 or CX3CL1 induce ERK1/2 phosphorylation in tm-chemokine expressing cells.
source: To find out, whether antibodies against the chemokine domains of CXCL16 or CX3CL1 can also induce signaling of the tm-chemokines, we stimulated stably transfected tm-CXCL16 or tm-CX3CL1 LOX cells with 0.1 µg/ml of the respective antibody (Figure 9A); IgG from the same species and mock-transfected cells served as controls. In fact, specific antibodies, but not controls induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation in tm-chemokine expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Monovalent F(ab) fragments of antibodies against chemokine domains do not induce signal transduction in tm-chemokine expressing cells.
source: However, monovalent F(ab) fragments of the same antibodies generated by papain digestion and purification did not produce any effects in transfected cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Di/oligomerization of tm-chemokines is necessary for signal transduction.
source: These experiments show that antibodies like soluble ligands induce signal transduction through tm-chemokines, and this process seems to depend on di/oligomerization of the tm-chemokines.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that intact antibodies but not monovalent F(ab) fragments induce signaling, as shown in Figure 9.

claim: Dimerization of the chemokine domain of CX3CL1 has been shown by X-ray crystal structure.
source: Similarly, di- and multimerization of the chemokine domain of CX3CL1 had already earlier been shown by X-ray crystal structure (Hoover et al., 2000), and is also known for some other (soluble) chemokines.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hoover et al., 2000.

claim: Clustering/bundle formation of transmembrane CX3CL1 has been observed in transfected and primary cells by bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) and homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF).
source: And indeed, a clustering/bundle formation of transmembrane CX3CL1 has been observed in transfected and primary cells by bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) and homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF; Hermand et al., 2008; Ostuni et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hermand et al., 2008 and Ostuni et al., 2014.

claim: The intracellular tails of transmembrane ligands contain signaling domains that are critical for signal transduction in reverse signaling.
source: Signaling domains of the intracellular tails of transmembrane ligands seem to be critical for the signal transduction in reverse signaling, and thus also may transduce inverse signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about reverse signaling mechanisms and is supported by the experimental data showing the requirement of intracellular domains for inverse signaling.

claim: TNF-α, FasL and other members of the TNF family contain S/TXXS/T sequences and proline-rich domains that can bind adaptor proteins and transduce signals.
source: For example, TNF-α, FasL and other members of the TNF family, contain S/TXXS/T sequences and proline-rich domains (FasL) that can bind adaptor proteins and thereby transduce signals (Kennelly and Krebs, 1991; Watts et al., 1999; Eissner et al., 2004; Sun and Fink, 2007; Amanchy et al., 2011; Daar, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kennelly and Krebs, 1991; Watts et al., 1999; Eissner et al., 2004; Sun and Fink, 2007; Amanchy et al., 2011; Daar, 2012).

claim: Ephrins and semaphorins signal through PDZ-binding motifs and proline-rich domains.
source: In contrast, ephrins and semaphorins signal through PDZ-binding motifs and also proline-rich domains (Klein, 2009; Zhou et al., 2008; Daar, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Klein, 2009; Zhou et al., 2008; Daar, 2012).

claim: Potential activation sites in transmembrane chemokines include cytoplasmic SXXS-sequences and SH2-binding sites (YXPV/R).
source: Potential activation sites include cytoplasmic SXXS-sequences (comparable to those of the TNF family) and additionally SH2-binding sites (YXPV/R).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis and comparison with known signaling motifs, as shown in Table 1.

claim: In CX3CL1, SXXS-sequences and SH2-binding sites are highly conserved from monotremes through marsupials to highly developed mammals.
source: In CX3CL1, both sites are highly conserved from monotremes through marsupials to highly developed mammals; in the case of CXCL16, they are found – as far as known - in primates and only same mammals (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Table 1.

claim: In CXCL16, SXXS-sequences and SH2-binding sites are found in primates and only some mammals.
source: In CX3CL1, both sites are highly conserved from monotremes through marsupials to highly developed mammals; in the case of CXCL16, they are found – as far as known - in primates and only same mammals (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Table 1.

claim: The expression of transmembrane chemokines can be induced by pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α, IFN-γ and interleukin-1β in fibroblasts and endothelial cells.
source: The expression of transmembrane chemokines can be induced by pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α, IFN-γ and interleukin-1β, e.g. in fibroblasts and endothelial cells (Garcia et al., 2000; Abel et al., 2004; Isozaki et al., 2011) regulating their role in inflammatory (trans-) migration processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Garcia et al., 2000; Abel et al., 2004; Isozaki et al., 2011).

claim: The release of the chemokine domain is mediated by the cell surface proteases ADAM10 and ADAM17 in a constitutive or cytokine-induced manner.
source: The release of the chemokine domain is mediated by the cell surface proteases ADAM10 and ADAM17 in a constitutive (mainly ADAM10) or cytokine-induced manner (Abel et al., 2004; Ludwig et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Abel et al., 2004; Ludwig et al., 2005).

claim: ADAM17 was initially discovered as TNF-α-converting enzyme (TACE) liberating soluble cytokine from the transmembrane form.
source: ADAM17 was initially discovered as TNF-α-converting enzyme (TACE) liberating soluble cytokine from the transmembrane form.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about ADAM17/TACE.

claim: ADAMs are supposed to terminate reverse signaling by cleaving transmembrane ligands of the TNF family bound to their receptors.
source: ADAMs are supposed to terminate reverse signaling by cleaving transmembrane ligands of the TNF family bound to their receptors (Sun and Fink, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sun and Fink, 2007.

claim: In the case of ephrin-A, ADAM10 is constitutively associated with the EphA receptor and cleaves ephrin-A5 in trans upon ligand binding.
source: In case of ephrin-A, ADAM10 is constitutively associated with the EphA receptor that clusters and is activated upon ligand binding; this positions the proteinase domain for effective ephrin-A5 cleavage and the cleavage occurs in trans, with ADAM10 and its substrate being on the membranes of opposing cells (Janes et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Janes et al., 2005.

claim: Inverse signaling is an autocrine feedback and fine-tuning system in the communication between cells.
source: We suppose that inverse signaling is an autocrine feedback and fine-tuning system in the communication between cells that in tumors supports stabilization and proliferation.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings regarding the biological role of inverse signaling.

claim: In tumors, inverse signaling supports stabilization and proliferation.
source: We suppose that inverse signaling is an autocrine feedback and fine-tuning system in the communication between cells that in tumors supports stabilization and proliferation.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation supported by the observed anti-apoptotic and proliferative effects in tumor cells shown in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: Inverse signaling appears to induce mainly autocrine stimulatory and stabilizing effects like increased proliferation and anti-apoptosis.
source: As far as we know, inverse signaling of transmembrane chemokines appears to induce mainly autocrine stimulatory and stabilizing effects like increased proliferation and anti-apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data showing proliferation enhancement and anti-apoptotic effects in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: Tumors would profit from the positive feedback provided by inverse signaling.
source: Obviously, tumors would clearly profit from such positive feedback.
evidence: This claim is a speculative inference based on the observed pro-survival and proliferative effects of inverse signaling in tumor cells.

claim: Autocrine loops are important in many types of tumors, as exemplified by growth factors like EGF or PDGF.
source: The importance of autocrine loops in many types of tumors becomes obvious regarding for example growth factors like epidermal (EGF) or platelet-derived (PDGF) growth factors.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about autocrine signaling in cancer biology.

claim: Stabilizing autocrine loops may play important roles in inflammation or under non-pathological conditions in tissue development.
source: However, also in inflammation or under non-pathological conditions in tissue development these stabilizing autocrine loops may play important roles.
evidence: This claim is a speculative extension of the findings to other biological contexts.

claim: Inverse signaling is a novel mechanism where soluble ligands shed from transmembrane counterparts induce signals through binding to the transmembrane ligands.
source: Inverse signaling is an autocrine feedback and fine-tuning systems in the communication between cells. Here, soluble ligands that are shed from their transmembrane counterparts induce signals through binding to the transmembrane ligands.
evidence: This claim summarizes the novel mechanism described throughout the manuscript and is supported by the collective experimental evidence.

claim: Reverse signaling requires the binding of the transmembrane ligand to its classical membrane-bound or soluble receptor.
source: Whereas reverse signaling requires the binding of the transmembrane ligand to its classical membrane-bound or soluble receptor, the inverse signaling depends on binding of the soluble ligand to its transmembrane counterpart.
evidence: This claim distinguishes inverse signaling from reverse signaling based on established knowledge about reverse signaling mechanisms.

claim: Inverse signaling depends on binding of the soluble ligand to its transmembrane counterpart.
source: Whereas reverse signaling requires the binding of the transmembrane ligand to its classical membrane-bound or soluble receptor, the inverse signaling depends on binding of the soluble ligand to its transmembrane counterpart.
evidence: This claim is supported by the binding experiments shown in Figure 5 and the functional studies throughout the manuscript.
